h1: When Do Baby Teeth Come In? Complete Timeline
description: Track your baby's teething timeline by age. See which of the 20 primary teeth should appear, what's next, and when to schedule the first dental visit.
seoKeywords: when do baby teeth come in
intro: Every parent has been there — your baby is drooling, fussing, chewing everything in sight, and you're wondering: is this a tooth coming in? Understanding the baby teeth eruption timeline can turn that guesswork into confidence. Human babies develop 20 primary teeth (also called baby teeth or deciduous teeth), and the process starts earlier than most people expect. The first tooth — usually a lower central incisor — typically breaks through the gum somewhere between 6 and 10 months of age. From there, new teeth arrive in a fairly predictable sequence, wrapping up around 30 to 33 months when the second molars settle in. But here's the thing: "typical" covers a wide range. Some babies sprout their first tooth at 4 months; others don't see one until after their first birthday. Both can be completely normal, and genetics plays a big role — if you or your partner were late teethers, your baby likely will be too. This calculator gives you a personalized eruption timeline based on your baby's current age in months. Enter their age and you'll instantly see: • Which teeth have most likely already come in • Which teeth are expected to emerge soon • How many teeth your baby should typically have right now • When to watch for the next teething wave Whether you're a first-time parent bracing for sleepless nights or a pediatrician looking for a quick reference tool, this timeline helps you stay one step ahead of the teething process — and know when something is worth a call to the dentist.
keyTakeaway: The **first tooth** typically appears around **6 months** (lower central incisor). By **12 months**, babies have ~6-8 teeth. By **2.5-3 years**, all **20 primary teeth** are complete.

explanation:
Human babies develop **20 primary teeth** (also called baby teeth or deciduous teeth) following a remarkably predictable sequence. The eruption window spans roughly **6 to 33 months**, with significant individual variation driven by genetics, prematurity, and nutritional factors. The American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry (AAPD) and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) both maintain reference timelines used by clinicians worldwide.

## How the timeline works

The calculator takes baby's age in months and compares it against the standard eruption ranges to estimate:

- Which teeth have most likely erupted by now.
- How many teeth the baby should have.
- Which teeth are next.
- Whether the schedule is on track (most pediatricians flag investigation only if no teeth by 15 months).

## Baby tooth eruption timeline

| Tooth | Eruption window (months) |
|---|---|
| Lower central incisors | 6-10 |
| Upper central incisors | 8-12 |
| Upper lateral incisors | 9-13 |
| Lower lateral incisors | 10-16 |
| Upper first molars | 13-19 |
| Lower first molars | 14-18 |
| Upper canines (cuspids) | 16-22 |
| Lower canines (cuspids) | 17-23 |
| Lower second molars | 23-31 |
| Upper second molars | 25-33 |

Total: **20 primary teeth** (10 upper + 10 lower). Lower teeth typically erupt slightly before their upper counterparts.

## Quick rule of thumb

Approximate number of teeth ≈ **age in months − 6** (valid roughly between 6 and 26 months). A 12-month-old should have around 6 teeth; a 22-month-old, around 16. This is a rough estimate — use the full table above for accuracy.

## Common teething symptoms

- Excessive drooling 4-8 weeks before eruption.
- Swollen, tender, or red gums.
- Increased irritability and chewing on objects.
- Sleep disruption around eruption days.
- **Mild** temperature elevation (< 38°C / 100.4°F).

A fever above 100.4°F is **not** caused by teething and warrants a pediatric evaluation — the AAP is explicit on this point.

## When to start dental care

- **Before first tooth**: wipe gums with a damp cloth or silicone finger brush after feeds.
- **First tooth through age 3**: soft infant toothbrush with a **rice-grain-sized smear of fluoride toothpaste**, twice daily.
- **Ages 3-6**: increase to a **pea-sized amount** of fluoride toothpaste, supervised spitting.
- **First dental visit**: by the first birthday or within 6 months of the first tooth, whichever comes first (AAPD recommendation).
- **Flossing**: start once two teeth touch each other.

## When to consult a pediatric dentist

- No teeth by **15 months** (rule out hypodontia or ectodermal dysplasia).
- Severe teething pain not responding to standard measures (cold teether, gentle gum massage).
- Teeth erupting severely misaligned or out of sequence.
- Decay on baby teeth (early childhood caries) — does not "heal" on its own and needs treatment.

faq.q: When does the first baby tooth typically come in?
faq.a: The first baby tooth usually emerges between 6 and 10 months of age. It's almost always one of the lower central incisors — the two bottom front teeth. Some babies cut their first tooth as early as 4 months; others don't see one until 12 or even 13 months. Both ends of this spectrum are generally considered normal. If no tooth has appeared by 15 months, the American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry recommends consulting a pediatric dentist to rule out developmental delays or hypodontia (missing tooth buds). Genetics is the strongest predictor — ask your parents when you got your first tooth.

faq.q: How many teeth should my baby have at each age?
faq.a: Here's a general guide based on typical eruption data: • 6 months: 0–2 teeth (may be none yet) • 9 months: 2–4 teeth • 12 months: 4–8 teeth • 18 months: 8–12 teeth • 24 months: 14–18 teeth • 30–33 months: All 20 primary teeth Remember, these are averages with wide normal ranges. A baby with 4 teeth at 12 months is just as normal as one with 8. The calculator factors in these ranges so you're not comparing your baby to a single "ideal" number.

faq.q: Is it normal if my baby has no teeth at 12 months?
faq.a: Yes, it can be completely normal. The first tooth normally erupts between 6 and 12 months, meaning some babies reach their first birthday without a single tooth. This is often hereditary — if you or your partner were late teethers, your child likely will be too. That said, if no teeth have appeared by 13 to 15 months, a visit to a pediatric dentist is a smart precaution. An X-ray can confirm that tooth buds are present and developing normally. Conditions like hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (which affects tooth development) are rare but worth ruling out with a professional evaluation.

This is one of the most common misconceptions in parenting. Teething does not cause high fevers. It may cause a very mild temperature elevation — studies suggest up to about 99–100°F (37.2–37.8°C) — due to localized gum inflammation. But a fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher is not caused by teething and should be evaluated by your child's doctor. The danger in blaming all fevers on teething is that real illnesses — ear infections, rosacea, urinary tract infections, viral infections — can go untreated. If your baby has a fever alongside teething symptoms, call your pediatrician.

faq.q: What can I give my baby for teething pain?
faq.a: Safe and effective options include: • Cold (not frozen) teething rings: The mild cold soothes gum inflammation. Frozen rings can damage gum tissue. • Gentle gum massage: Use a clean finger to apply light pressure to the gum for 1–2 minutes. • Age-appropriate pain relievers: Acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (for babies 6 months+) can help — always dose by weight per your pediatrician's instructions. Avoid: • Benzocaine gels (products like Orajel) — the FDA warns against use in children under 2 due to risk of methemoglobinemia • Homeopathic teething tablets containing belladonna • Amber teething necklaces — choking and strangulation hazard with no proven benefit

faq.q: When do baby teeth fall out?
faq.a: Primary teeth begin to shed around age 5 to 7, usually starting with the lower central incisors — the same teeth that erupted first. The shedding process mirrors the eruption sequence and is typically complete by ages 12 to 13. The order: incisors first, then canines and premolars, then second molars. Permanent (adult) teeth begin replacing them during this same window. If a baby tooth is lost significantly early due to decay or injury, a space maintainer may be recommended by a dentist to prevent neighboring teeth from drifting and crowding the incoming permanent tooth.

faq.q: Does my baby need a dental visit before age 1?
faq.a: Yes. Both the American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry (AAPD) and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommend a child's first dental visit by their first birthday, or within 6 months of the first tooth erupting — whichever comes first. This early visit accomplishes several things: the dentist checks that eruption is progressing normally, applies fluoride varnish to protect early teeth, evaluates bite development, and coaches parents on brushing technique, diet, and pacifier/bottle habits. Early dental visits are strongly associated with lower rates of early childhood caries (cavities).

faq.q: Does breastfeeding affect my baby's teeth?
faq.a: Breastfeeding supports healthy jaw and palate development and is beneficial overall. However, breast milk — like formula and cow's milk — contains lactose (a sugar) that can contribute to tooth decay if teeth are in prolonged contact with it. This is particularly true when babies fall asleep at the breast or with a bottle, a pattern known as baby bottle tooth decay or early childhood caries. To reduce risk: after the last nighttime feeding, wipe your baby's gums or teeth with a damp cloth or soft toothbrush. Once teeth erupt, avoid letting your baby sleep with a bottle of formula, juice, or milk.

faq.q: Why do some teeth cause more pain than others?
faq.a: Not all teething is equal. Central incisors (the first teeth) and lateral incisors tend to cause relatively mild discomfort because they're flat-edged and push through gum tissue more easily. Canines (cuspids), which erupt around 16–23 months, are notoriously painful — their pointed, conical shape requires more force to cut through. The first and second molars (12–33 months) are wide, flat teeth pushing through a larger gum surface area, which can cause the most discomfort of all. Many parents report that molar teething coincides with more sleep disruption, increased drooling, and more clingy behavior.

faq.q: What is the full order of baby teeth eruption?
faq.a: The 20 primary teeth typically erupt in this order (ages are approximate): 1. Lower central incisors — 6–10 months 2. Upper central incisors — 8–12 months 3. Upper lateral incisors — 9–13 months 4. Lower lateral incisors — 10–16 months 5. Upper first molars — 13–19 months 6. Lower first molars — 14–18 months 7. Upper canines (cuspids) — 16–22 months 8. Lower canines (cuspids) — 17–23 months 9. Lower second molars — 23–31 months 10. Upper second molars — 25–33 months The lower teeth often erupt slightly before their upper counterparts.

faq.q: Should I be concerned if teeth come in crooked?
faq.a: Not immediately. Baby teeth often erupt slightly crooked or with gaps and then self-correct as surrounding teeth emerge and the jaw grows. Small gaps between baby teeth are actually a good sign — they make room for the larger permanent teeth coming later. However, if teeth are severely misaligned, overlapping, or if your child has habits like prolonged pacifier use or thumb-sucking past age 3, mention it to your pediatric dentist. Early orthodontic assessments (called interceptive orthodontics) can sometimes address bite issues before they become more complex.

faq.q: How do I clean my baby's teeth and gums?
faq.a: Start oral hygiene before teeth even appear: • Before first tooth: Wipe gums with a soft, damp cloth or silicone finger brush after feedings. • First tooth through age 3: Use a soft-bristled infant toothbrush with a rice-grain-sized smear of fluoride toothpaste twice daily. • Ages 3–6: Increase to a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste; supervise to ensure they spit, not swallow. • Start flossing once two teeth are touching each other. The ADA recommends brushing for 2 minutes, twice a day. Making it a consistent routine early — even if your baby fusses — sets the foundation for lifelong oral health.
